title: Failure
summary: Name timeouts, retries, and idempotency for one hop that will fail.

parts.rule: Pick one critical hop and specify timeout, retry policy, backoff, and idempotency. Retries without idempotency create duplicate side effects. Timeouts without retries leave clients hanging on hung sockets. Prefer fail-fast with a budget over infinite waits. Say what the user sees when the hop is down.
parts.why: Happy-path-only designs melt on the first blip. Interviewers almost always ask "what if this call fails?" A concrete timeout-plus-retry-plus-idempotency answer beats a vague "we are highly available."
parts.example: Checkout calls Billing with a 200 ms timeout. On timeout or 503, retry up to two times with exponential backoff (50 ms, 100 ms) and the same Idempotency-Key header so a double charge cannot land twice. After exhaustion, return 503 to the client with a stable error code and do not pretend success. For redirect cache fills, a failed Redis GET simply falls through to the database — degrade, do not error the user. Circuit breaker: if Billing error rate exceeds fifty percent for thirty seconds, open the circuit and fail fast for a cool-down instead of stampeding. Always bound total retry time inside the user's request budget. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism.
parts.use: Apply this template to every synchronous dependency on the user path. Use idempotency keys on any retried write. Use degrade-to-DB or degrade-to-stale for non-critical caches.
parts.refuse: Refuse infinite retries on user-facing threads. Refuse retries on non-idempotent writes without a key. Refuse omitting timeouts ("wait until the library default"). Refuse claiming perfect uptime instead of naming the degraded mode.

body:
Rule. Pick one critical hop and specify timeout, retry policy, backoff, and idempotency. Retries without idempotency create duplicate side effects. Timeouts without retries leave clients hanging on hung sockets. Prefer fail-fast with a budget over infinite waits. Say what the user sees when the hop is down.

Why it matters. Happy-path-only designs melt on the first blip. Interviewers almost always ask "what if this call fails?" A concrete timeout-plus-retry-plus-idempotency answer beats a vague "we are highly available."

Worked example. Checkout calls Billing with a 200 ms timeout. On timeout or 503, retry up to two times with exponential backoff (50 ms, 100 ms) and the same Idempotency-Key header so a double charge cannot land twice. After exhaustion, return 503 to the client with a stable error code and do not pretend success. For redirect cache fills, a failed Redis GET simply falls through to the database — degrade, do not error the user. Circuit breaker: if Billing error rate exceeds fifty percent for thirty seconds, open the circuit and fail fast for a cool-down instead of stampeding. Always bound total retry time inside the user's request budget. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism.

[[diagram:blast]]

When to use. Apply this template to every synchronous dependency on the user path. Use idempotency keys on any retried write. Use degrade-to-DB or degrade-to-stale for non-critical caches.

When to refuse. Refuse infinite retries on user-facing threads. Refuse retries on non-idempotent writes without a key. Refuse omitting timeouts ("wait until the library default"). Refuse claiming perfect uptime instead of naming the degraded mode.
